newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU snub could undermine West's role in Turkey.
newsitem.headline: EU snub could undermine West's role in Turkey.

text.p: Europe's latest rebuff of Turkey's aspirations for EU membership risks undermining pro-Western elements battling against growing Islamist influence in the key strategic NATO ally, analysts say.

"This could well have a negative impact and dishearten pro-Western elements," said Shireen Hunter of the Brussels-based thinktank, the Centre For European Policy Studies. "It could backfire on attempts to further democratise Turkey."

In the clearest signal yet that Turkey's hopes of eventual membership of the European Union were misplaced, centre-right leaders, including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, have said Ankara should instead be content with a special relationship.

"We are creating a European Union. That is a European project," said Wilfried Martens, president of the European People's Party and a former prime minister of Belgium, adding it was "not acceptable" for Turkey to join.
Martens was speaking after a one-day meeting of the pan-European grouping of centre-right parties and diplomats said his remarks had been endorsed by Kohl, the EU's single most influential leader.
The centre-right parties apparently agreed unanimously that Turkey's human rights record, its size and its Moslem religion disqualified it from joining the European club.

Independent analysts said European Union countries now had to spell out what type of relationship they foresee with the giant Moslem country on its vulnerable southern rim or risk seeing Ankara turn its back on what it sees as an ungrateful West.

"This is a terrible blow for the Turkish elite, their aspirations are simply not taken seriously by the EU and people will start saying we have to look elsewhere for a real partnership," said one senior diplomatic source.

Turkey, its secularist military already coexisting uneasily with the Islamist-led government of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, feels it has not been rewarded for its loyalty to the West throughout the Cold War and, more recently, the Gulf War.

Hunter and other analysts fear that if all hope of EU membership is removed the pro-Western elite, which has spent years trying to bring the country closer to Europe, will lose more ground and make the country more stable.

"With all hope of membership gone, some could argue there is less need for restraint," Hunter said, adding the pro-western military would not lead a coup against an elected government, even an Islamist one, while EU membership was a possibility.

Diplomats said Washington, which has been urging the EU to pay more attention to Turkey, was aghast at the latest snub to Ankara, fearing it could further poison relations with Greece and damage attempts to solve the long-running Cyprus dispute.

EU states had hoped a historic customs union with Turkey, finally approved last year, would go some way to assuaging Turkish anger over the fact that former communist countries in eastern Europe had jumped ahead in the queue for EU membership.

The EU has said membership negotiations with those countries, led by Poland and Hungary, could open some six months after the end of this year's review of EU treaties. Ankara has pushed for a similar commitment.
Last month, Turkey threatened to block NATO's planned eastwards enlargement later this year unless it was invited along with other candidate countries to this year's EU summit in Amsterdam in June.
Meanwhile, Greece has blocked the dispersal of funds under the customs union.

"The customs pact has been a huge disappointment. Meanwhile countries with less developed economies, such as Bulgaria, and who were on the other side in the Cold War, appear to have more chance of (EU) membership," said another analyst.

Washington, increasingly concerned about instability on Turkey's doorstep in Central Asia, is angered the Europeans have not yet come out with a real strategy for countries on its Mediterranean rim which cannot gain membership.
